questions.q: Once a prompt is tokenized, what is the primary function of a base (foundation) LLM?
options: To predict the next token in the sequence
To check facts against a database
To translate the prompt into code
questions.explain: Base models complete text token by token; instruction tuning makes them follow requests.
questions.evidence: the primary function of the "Base LLM" (or Foundation model) is to predict the token in that sequence.

questions.q: Besides giving examples, which technique uses primary content to steer the model?
options: Writing the prompt in capital letters
questions.explain: A cue (for example the start of the desired output) nudges the model toward the format you want.
questions.evidence: Another technique for using primary content is to provide cues rather than examples.

questions.q: What does the quality of results from a prompt depend on?
options: Only on which model you use
How much information you provide and how well-crafted the prompt is
How long you wait before sending it
questions.explain: Instructions, context, inputs and examples all improve results.
questions.evidence: the quality of results depends on how much information you provide it and how well-crafted the prompt is.

questions.q: What is Top P?
options: The maximum number of tokens in a reply
A ranking of the best models
A sampling technique (nucleus sampling) that controls how deterministic the model is
questions.explain: Lower Top P (or temperature) gives more deterministic, factual answers; higher gives more varied ones.
questions.evidence: Top P - A sampling technique with temperature, called nucleus sampling, where you can control how deterministic the model is.

questions.q: What does the guide recommend about the context you give in a prompt?
options: The more specific and relevant to the task, the better
Always keep it under ten words
Leave it out so the model can be creative
Use the same context for every task
questions.explain: Specific, relevant detail matters most when you want a particular outcome or style.
questions.evidence: Usually, the more specific and relevant the context is to the task you are trying to perform, the better.

questions.q: Why is prompting described as an 'emergent property' of an LLM?
options: Because prompts only work in emergencies
Because the model was explicitly programmed to follow prompts
Because it is not a feature built into the model but something we discover as we use it
Because prompts are generated by the model itself
questions.explain: That is why prompt techniques are found by experimentation.
questions.evidence: prompting is an emergent property of an LLM meaning that this is not a feature that is built into the model but rather something we discover as we use the model.

questions.q: What is zero-shot prompting?
options: A prompt that has zero words
A prompt with no examples or demonstrations
A prompt that is sent without an API key
A prompt that always gets a wrong answer
questions.explain: Few-shot prompting adds a handful of examples; zero-shot relies on instructions alone.
questions.evidence: Zero-shot prompting means that the prompt used to interact with the model won't contain examples or demonstrations.

questions.q: Chain-of-thought prompting can be combined with which technique to do better on complex reasoning tasks?
questions.explain: Worked examples that show their reasoning help the model reason step by step.
questions.evidence: You can combine it with few-shot prompting to get better results on more complex tasks that require reasoning before responding.

questions.q: How does prompt chaining work?
options: A task is split into subtasks, and each response is used as input to the next prompt
The same prompt is sent many times and the answers are averaged
Several users write one prompt together
The model is asked to ignore its earlier answers
questions.explain: Breaking work into steps makes LLM pipelines more reliable and easier to debug.
questions.evidence: Once those subtasks have been identified, the LLM is prompted with a subtask and then its response is used as input to another prompt.

questions.q: Why is it important to protect against prompt attacks such as prompt injection?
options: They could bypass safety guardrails and break the model's guiding principles
questions.explain: User input is mixed with your instructions, so untrusted text can try to override them.
questions.evidence: it's really important to protect against prompt attacks that could bypass safety guardrails and break the guiding principles of the model.

questions.q: What is tokenisation?
options: Converting text into smaller units (tokens) a model can process
Counting the words in a document
questions.explain: Models predict the next token in a sequence.
questions.evidence: Tokenization: The process of converting text into smaller units, called tokens, that a model can understand and process.

questions.q: What two steps make up prompt engineering?
options: Buying a model, then training it
Designing an initial prompt, then refining it iteratively
questions.explain: It is a trial-and-error process that needs intuition and effort.
questions.evidence: designing the initial prompt for a given model and objective refining the prompt iteratively to improve the quality of the response

questions.q: What does the course mean by 'fabrication'?
options: Building a new model from scratch
An LLM generating factually incorrect information
questions.explain: It stems from limits in training data and other constraints.
questions.evidence: the phenomenon where LLMs sometimes generate factually incorrect information due to limitations in their training or other constraints

questions.q: Why does the course prefer the word 'fabrication' to 'hallucination'?
options: To avoid giving a machine a human-like trait
questions.explain: The wording keeps the focus on a machine-driven outcome.
questions.evidence: so we don't accidentally anthropomorphize the behavior by attributing a human-like trait to a machine-driven outcome

questions.q: What can reduce model fabrications to some extent?
options: Techniques like metaprompting and temperature settings
questions.explain: They help but don't eliminate the problem — always check facts.
questions.evidence: Prompt engineering techniques like metaprompting and temperature configuration may reduce model fabrications to some extent.

questions.q: What does Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF) train a model to do?
options: Follow instructions and learn from feedback
questions.explain: Instruction-tuned models give answers better suited to practical use.
questions.evidence: techniques like Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF) that can train the model to follow instructions and learn from feedback

questions.q: What is a prompt template?
options: The first prompt a user ever writes
A reusable, pre-defined recipe for a prompt, with placeholders
questions.explain: Templates give consistent experiences at scale.
questions.evidence: A prompt template is a pre-defined recipe for a prompt that can be stored and reused as needed, to drive more consistent user experiences at scale.

questions.q: What is supporting (secondary) content in a prompt?
options: Additional context provided to influence the output
questions.explain: It sits alongside the instruction and the primary content.
questions.evidence: secondary content is like additional context we provide to influence the output in some way

questions.q: Which approach do practitioners recommend starting with?
options: Zero-shot, then refining with a few examples (few-shot)
questions.explain: Add examples only when the instruction alone isn't enough.
questions.evidence: Start with a zero-shot approach where you give it an instruction (but no examples) then try few-shot as a refinement

questions.q: What does adding more examples in a few-shot prompt do?
options: Helps the model make more accurate inferences without extra instructions
questions.explain: The model infers the pattern from the examples.
questions.evidence: The few-shot example shows how adding more examples allows models to make more accurate inferences with no added instructions.

questions.q: Why is it good practice to make prompt instructions specific?
options: The more specific the instruction, the better the results
It hides the task from the model
questions.explain: Components like role or format are optional but help.
questions.evidence: the more specific you are with instruction, the better results you will get

questions.q: Which tasks does the 'Examples of Prompts' guide cover?
options: Summarisation, extraction, question answering, classification, conversation, code and reasoning
questions.explain: Each needs slightly different prompt design.
questions.evidence: Topics: Text Summarization Information Extraction Question Answering Text Classification Conversation Code Generation Reasoning

questions.q: When is giving the model an identity and behaviour (e.g. a research assistant) particularly useful?
options: When building conversational systems like customer service chatbots
questions.explain: The role shapes tone and content of every reply.
questions.evidence: This is particularly useful when you are building conversational systems like customer service chatbots.

questions.q: What two steps does writing prompts involve?
options: Constructing the prompt with relevant context, then gradually optimising it
questions.explain: Even good techniques usually need optimising.
questions.evidence: constructing the prompt, by providing relevant context, and optimization

questions.q: What does chain-of-thought prompting tell the LLM?
options: How to break a problem down into steps
questions.explain: It fixed the apple-counting example the model first got wrong.
questions.evidence: Chain-of-thought , this type of prompting tells the LLM how to break down a problem into steps.

questions.q: What does the least-to-most technique do?
options: Asks the model to critique itself
Breaks a problem into steps and asks for them to be done in order
questions.explain: It is similar to chain-of-thought.
questions.evidence: this technique is about breaking down a problem into a series of steps and then ask these steps to be performed in order

questions.q: What does the self-refine technique involve?
options: Asking the LLM to critique its own answer
questions.explain: Critique often reveals flaws to fix in a better answer.
questions.evidence: a good idea is to ask the LLM to critique itself, which leads us to the self-refine technique

questions.q: Which setting makes model output more predictable (deterministic) or more varied?
questions.explain: Lower temperature gives more predictable output.
questions.evidence: Using temperature to vary your output

questions.q: What tendency do LLMs have regarding factuality?
options: They refuse to answer factual questions
They can produce coherent, convincing answers that are made up
questions.explain: Better prompts and ground truth reduce this risk.
questions.evidence: LLMs have a tendency to generate responses that sounds coherent and convincing but can sometimes be made up.

questions.q: How can better prompts help with factuality?
options: They guarantee every answer is true
They can make responses more accurate and reduce made-up answers
questions.explain: For example, asking the model to admit when it doesn't know.
questions.evidence: Improving prompts can help improve the model to generate more accurate/factual responses and reduce the likelihood to generate inconsistent and made up responses.

questions.q: In few-shot learning, what question does the lesson test about the exemplars?
options: Whether their distribution biases the model
Whether they are in alphabetical order
questions.explain: Skewed examples can push answers one way.
questions.evidence: When performing few-shot learning, does the distribution of the exemplars affect the performance of the model or bias the model in some way?

questions.q: How does a prompt injection attack work?
options: It floods the server with traffic
It injects an instruction to ignore the original one and follow the attacker's
questions.explain: It hijacks the model's output, possibly to produce harmful content.
questions.evidence: it hijacks the model output by injecting an instruction to ignore the original instruction and execute the injected one

questions.q: Prompt injection is similar to which classic attack, whose defences may help?
questions.explain: Both mix untrusted input with instructions.
questions.evidence: Prompt injections have similarities to SQL injection and we can potentially learn defense tactics from that domain.

questions.q: What is jailbreaking a model?
options: Bypassing its safety policies and guardrails
Upgrading it to a new version
questions.explain: Newer models resist many techniques but still have flaws.
questions.evidence: it is still possible to bypass those safety policies and guardrails using different jailbreaking techniques

questions.q: What does the guide advise to avoid prompt leaks?
options: Be very careful about what you pass in prompts
questions.explain: Confidential instructions or data in a prompt can be extracted.
questions.evidence: The advise here is to be very careful of what you are passing in prompts

questions.q: Why are LLM applications vulnerable to prompt injection?
options: Models are always connected to the internet
Instructions and user input are chained with no standard format the model expects
questions.explain: That flexibility is useful but creates vulnerabilities.
questions.evidence: there is no standard format that the model expects
